title: God's Weird Real Estate Deal in a War Zone
paragraphs: So, here's the 411 God gave Jeremiah in the tenth year Zedekiah was king of Judah. This was also the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign. At this point, the Babylonian army had Jerusalem on total lockdown, and Jeremiah was locked up in the royal palace jail. King Zedekiah of Judah threw him in there, all mad, like, “How dare you go around prophesying, saying, ‘God says, I’m telling you, I’m handing this city over to the king of Babylon, and he’s gonna take it. And King Zedekiah will be handed over to the Babylonians too. He’ll have to face the music. He’s getting shipped off to Babylon and will stay there until I deal with him. That's a decree from God. So go ahead and fight the Babylonians, see how well that works out for you—it won’t.’”

Jeremiah said, “Then God’s message hit me, just like this: Get ready! Your cousin Hanamel, son of your uncle Shallum, is coming to you. He’s gonna say, ‘Buy my field in Anathoth. It's your family right to buy it first.’”

“And for real, just like God said, my cousin Hanamel showed up at the jail and said, ‘Hey, buy my field in Anathoth, in the Benjamin territory. You’ve got the legal right to keep it in the family. Buy it. Take it.’”
“That was it. I knew for sure it was a message from God.”

“So I bought the field in Anathoth from my cousin Hanamel. I paid him seventeen silver shekels. I did all the official stuff: wrote up the bill of sale, sealed it, and weighed out the silver in front of witnesses. Then I took the deed—the sealed copy with the contract and all the fine print, plus the open copy—and gave them to Baruch, son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah. This all went down in front of my cousin Hanamel, the witnesses who signed the deed, and all the other Jews who were hanging around the jail that day.”

“Then, in front of everyone, I told Baruch, ‘This is an order from the God-of-the-Angel-Armies, the God of Israel: Take these documents—both the sealed one and the open one—and stick them in a clay jar to keep them safe. Because the God-of-the-Angel-Armies, the God of Israel, says, “Life is gonna get back to normal. People are going to be buying houses and fields and vineyards in this country again.”’”

“After I handed the legal papers to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to God, ‘Okay, God, my Master, you literally created the heavens and the earth with your insane power—just by stretching out your arm! There’s lowkey nothing you can’t do. You show loyal love to thousands, but you also make kids deal with the consequences of their parents’ screw-ups. You’re the great and powerful God, the God-of-the-Angel-Armies, you have a plan and you always follow through. You see everything people do and you give them what they deserve, based on how they live and what they do.’”

“‘You did some wild signs and wonders back in Egypt and you’re still doing them today, right here in Israel and everywhere else. You’ve made a name for yourself that’s still legendary. You brought your people Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders—a crazy powerful rescue!—just by stretching out your arm. You gave them this land, a super rich and fertile place you promised their ancestors. But when they got here and took it over, they didn’t listen to you. They didn’t follow your rules. They ignored everything you told them. And that’s why you brought this whole disaster on them.’”

“‘And now, just look—the siege ramps are already up against the city to capture it. Death, starvation, and sickness are here. The Babylonians are attacking! What you said would happen is happening—it’s literally the daily news! And yet, God, my Master, even though the city is 100% going to be handed over to the Babylonians, you still told me, ‘Buy the field. Pay cash for it. And make sure you get witnesses.’ Make it make sense.’”

Then God’s message came to Jeremiah again: “Yo, pay attention! I am God, the God of every living thing. Is there anything I can’t do? So listen up, here’s God’s message: No doubt, I’m handing this city over to the Babylonians and their king, Nebuchadnezzar. He’s gonna take it. The attacking Babylonians will break in and burn the city to the ground: all those houses where people used their roofs as altars to burn offerings to Baal and worship a bunch of other random gods. That really ticked me off. It’s not like this is new. The people of Israel and Judah have been doing stuff I hate for a long, long time, making me angry with their lifestyle. That’s God’s decree.”

“This city has made me mad since the day it was built, and now I’m just done. I’m destroying it. I can’t even look at the wicked lives of the people of Israel and Judah anymore. They’ve been intentionally making me angry, all of them—kings, leaders, priests, prophets, everyone in the country and the city. They’ve turned their backs on me—won’t even look at me!—even though I tried so hard to teach them how to live. They just wouldn’t listen, refused to learn. They even put their disgusting idol statues in the very Temple that was built for me—that’s a wild level of disrespect! Then they built shrines to the god Baal in the Hinnom valley, where they burned their own kids as sacrifices to the god Molech—I can’t even wrap my head around that kind of evil!—turning the whole country into one giant sin.”
“But I, the God of Israel, also have this message for this city, the one you’re all saying ‘is being handed over to the king of Babylon through war, starvation, and disease’:

“‘Watch this! I’m going to gather them back from all the countries where I scattered them in my anger and fury. Yeah, I’ll bring them all back to this place and let them live in peace. They will be my people, and I will be their God. I’ll give them a single purpose and a united heart to always respect me, so they and their kids can have good, full lives. On top of that, I’ll make a forever promise with them, a covenant to always stick with them and do good for them. I’ll put a deep respect for me in their hearts so they won’t even think about leaving me.’”
“‘Oh, I’m going to be so happy for them! I’ll be so stoked to do good things for them! With my whole heart and soul, I’ll plant them in this land and make sure they stay here!’”

“‘Yep, this is God’s message: ‘Just as I brought this massive disaster on these people, I’m also going to bring them an amazing, prosperous life. I promise. People are going to buy fields here again, yes, in this very country that you think is a lost cause—a wasteland, destroyed by the Babylonians. Yes, people will buy farms again, legally, with deeds and sealed documents and proper witnesses—right here in the territory of Benjamin, around Jerusalem, in the towns of Judah, the hill country, the western foothills, and the Negev. I will restore everything that was lost.’ That’s God’s decree.”

title: God's Epic Comeback Plan for Jerusalem
paragraphs: So, while Jeremiah was still locked up in jail, God sent him another message. It was wild.

God, the one who literally made the earth, made it a livable place, and is known everywhere as GOD, said this: 'Yo, call out to me, and I'll answer you. I'll tell you some legit amazing and mind-blowing things that you could never figure out on your own.'

'Here's the deal with what's happening in this city,' said God, the God of Israel. 'You see the houses and even the king's palaces all torn down because of the war with the Chaldeans? You see the streets filled with the bodies of people I had to take out because of my righteous anger? It's all because the evil stuff happening in this city made me sick to my stomach.'

'But hold up, take another look. I'm about to give this city a total glow-up, a real healing from the inside out. I'm going to show them what a full life, packed with blessings, looks like. I'll restore everything that Judah and Jerusalem lost. I'll build it all back, good as new. I'll scrub them clean from all the dirt of their sins against me. I'll forgive everything they did wrong, all their rebellious phases. And Jerusalem will be a place of joy, praise, and glory that every country on earth will hear about. They'll get the news about all the good things I'm doing for her, and they'll be in total awe of the insane blessings I'm pouring on her.'

'Yep, God's message is this: You're looking at this place, these empty and trashed towns in Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, and you're thinking, "It's a wasteland. No one can live here. Not even a dog." But the time is coming when you'll hear laughter and parties, wedding celebrations, and people shouting, "Thank God-of-the-Angel-Armies! He's so good! His love never quits!" as they bring thank-you offerings to God's Temple. I'll restore everything this land lost. I'll make it all as good as new. I, God, promise you that.'

'The God-of-the-Angel-Armies says: This place that's a total wasteland, not even fit for a stray dog, is going to be a pasture for shepherds and their flocks again. You'll see flocks everywhere—in the mountains, in the towns of the Shephelah and the Negev, all over Benjamin's territory, around Jerusalem, and in the towns of Judah. Flocks looked after by shepherds who keep track of every single sheep. God says so.'

'Watch for this: The time is coming,'—this is God's decree—'when I'm going to keep the promise I made to the families of Israel and Judah. When that time comes, I'll raise up a fresh and true leader from David's family line. He will run this country with honesty and fairness. He will make things right. That's when Judah will be safe, and Jerusalem will live in security. The city's motto will be, "God Has Made Things Right for Us." God has made it crystal clear that there will always be a descendant of David ruling the people of Israel, and there will always be Levitical priests to handle the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and all the sacrificial worship in my honor.'

God's message came to Jeremiah: 'God says, If my deal with the day and my deal with the night ever fell apart, so that day and night just became random and you never knew what was coming, then and only then would my deal with my servant David fall apart, and his descendants would no longer rule. The same goes for the Levitical priests who serve me. Just like you can't count the stars in the sky or measure the sand on the seashore, you won't be able to count the descendants of my servant David and the Levites who serve me.'

God's message to Jeremiah continued: 'Have you heard the rumors going around? People are saying, "Those two families God chose, Israel and Judah, he totally disowned them." And have you noticed how my people are being treated with contempt, with whispers that they're a nobody nation now?'

'Well, here's God's comeback: If my covenant with day and night wasn't working, if the sky and earth weren't running the way I set them up, then, and only then, you might think I had disowned the descendants of Jacob and my servant David, and that I wouldn't put any of David's kids in charge of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But as it is, I will give them back everything they've lost. The final word is, I will have mercy on them.'

title: Promises Are Made to Be... Kept?
paragraphs: So, God hit up Jeremiah with a message while King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon was going all out, attacking Jerusalem and all the towns around it. Nebuchadnezzar brought his whole army, all his allies, and basically anyone he could find.

God, the God of Israel, was like, "Yo, go tell Zedekiah, the king of Judah: 'Listen up, this is God's message. I'm about to hand this city over to the king of Babylon, and he's gonna burn it to the ground. And don't even think you're getting away. You'll be captured and become his prisoner. You'll have a face-to-face with the king of Babylon and then get dragged off to Babylon as a captive.'

"'But chill for a sec, Zedekiah, and listen to the rest of God's message. You won't get killed in some crazy way. You'll actually die peacefully. They'll even honor you with a big funeral, just like they did for the kings who came before you. They'll genuinely mourn for you, crying, "Our leader, our leader!" This is a legit promise. God's word.'"

The prophet Jeremiah passed on this exact message to King Zedekiah in Jerusalem. This was all happening while the king of Babylon was in the middle of his huge attack on Jerusalem and the last few standing cities in Judah—which turned out to be just Lachish and Azekah (they were the only fortified cities left).

Then God sent another message to Jeremiah. This was after King Zedekiah had made a big pact with the people of Jerusalem to free all the Hebrew slaves, both men and women. The deal was that no one in Judah would own a fellow Jew as a slave. All the leaders and the people who signed on to this pact actually set their slaves free.
But then, a little while later, they totally went back on their word, broke their promise, and forced their former slaves to be slaves all over again. Lowkey messed up.

Then Jeremiah got this message from God: "God, the God of Israel, says, 'I made a covenant with your ancestors when I got them out of slavery in Egypt. Back then, I made it crystal clear: "At the end of seven years, every one of you has to free any fellow Hebrew who had to sell himself to you. After he's served you for six years, you set him free." But your ancestors completely ignored me.'

"'And now, you guys—what did you do? First, you got back on the right track and did the right thing. You declared freedom for your brothers and sisters and even made it official with a serious promise in my own Temple. And then you did a complete 180, broke your word, and made a mockery of me and the covenant. You forced all those men and women you had just set free right back into slavery.

"'So here's what I, God, have to say about that: You didn't obey me and set your brothers and sisters free. So here's what I'm gonna do: I'm gonna set *you* free—God's decree—free to be killed in war, or by disease, or by starvation. I'm going to make you a horror story. People all over the world will take one look at you and freak out. Everyone who broke my covenant, who didn't stick to the promise they made when they cut that young bull in half and walked between the pieces—all those people, the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, the palace officials, the priests, and everyone else—I'm handing them all over to their enemies who are trying to kill them. Their dead bodies will become food for vultures and stray dogs.

"'As for Zedekiah king of Judah and his palace crew, I'll hand them over to their enemies too, the ones who want them dead. The Babylonian army might have backed off for a little while, but not for long. I'm about to give the order that brings them right back to this city. They'll attack it, capture it, and burn it to the ground. The towns around Judah won't do any better. I'll turn them into ghost towns, totally unlivable.'" That's God's decree.

title: This One Family Kept a Promise for 200 Years & God Noticed
paragraphs: A message from God came to Jeremiah about ten years ago, back when Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, was king of Judah.
God was like, "Go find the Recabite crew. Invite them for a meeting in one of the rooms at the Temple, and offer them some wine."

So, I went and found Jaazaniah (son of another Jeremiah, who was the son of Habazziniah), and brought him, all his brothers, and his sons—basically the entire Recabite family—to the Temple. We went to the meeting room of Hanan, son of Igdaliah, who was a man of God. His room was right next to the office of the Temple big shots and just above the apartment of Maaseiah, son of Shallum, the guy in charge of the Temple.
Then I put out a bunch of cups and pitchers of wine for the Recabites and was like, "Let's make a toast! Drink up!"

But they were totally not having it. "We don't drink wine," they said. "Our ancestor, Jonadab son of Recab, gave us a command: 'You and your kids are never, ever to drink wine. And don't build houses, or settle down and plant fields or vineyards. Don't even own property. Just live in tents like nomads, so you can live a long and good life on the move.'

"And we've actually done it. We've followed every single thing our ancestor Jonadab son of Recab commanded. Me, our wives, our sons, our daughters—none of us drink wine. We don't build houses, own vineyards, or have fields or gardens. We live in tents, always moving. We listened to our ancestor Jonadab and did everything he told us to do.

"But, lowkey, the only reason we're in Jerusalem right now is because King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon invaded. We were like, 'Okay, let's dip to Jerusalem to dodge the Babylonian and Aramean armies and find a safe spot.' That's the whole story of why we're here."

Then God gave Jeremiah another message: "The Lord of Angel Armies, the God of Israel, wants you to go tell the people of Judah and Jerusalem, 'Why can't you guys learn a lesson and just do what I say?' This is God's decree. 'The commands Jonadab son of Recab gave his kids have been followed perfectly. He told them not to drink wine, and they haven't had a single drop to this day. They respected and obeyed their ancestor's command. But look at you! I've gone out of my way to get your attention, and you've just straight up ignored me. I sent prophet after prophet, all my servants, telling you from morning 'til night to change your ways, to make a clean break from your messed-up past and do what's right. I told you not to chase after every new god that pops up, but to settle down and be faithful in this land I gave your ancestors.'
"'And what do I get back from you? Nothing. You've completely ignored me. The descendants of Jonadab son of Recab did exactly what their ancestor told them, but my own people ignore me.'

"So, this is what's about to happen. The Lord of Angel Armies, the God of Israel, says, 'I'm going to bring a total disaster down on the people of Judah and Jerusalem—the exact disaster I warned you about—because you wouldn't listen when I spoke and you turned your backs on me when I called.'"

Then, turning to the Recabite community, Jeremiah said, "And this is what the Lord of Angel Armies, the God of Israel, says to you: 'Because you did what your ancestor Jonadab told you, obeyed his commands, and followed all his instructions, listen to this message from the Lord of Angel Armies, the God of Israel: There will always be a descendant of Jonadab son of Recab serving me! Always!'"

title: King Burns God's Message, God Hits 'Resend'
paragraphs: Alright, so check it. In the fourth year that Jehoiakim was king of Judah, God sent a message to Jeremiah.

God was like, 'Get a scroll and write down everything I've told you about Israel, Judah, and all the other nations, from the very first time I spoke to you back in Josiah's reign all the way to today.'

'The idea is that maybe the people of Judah will finally get the picture, you know? Realize the huge disaster I have planned for them, turn back from their messed-up lives, and actually let me forgive all their sin and rebellion.'
So Jeremiah called up his guy, Baruch. Jeremiah dictated, and Baruch wrote down every single word God had told him on a scroll.

Then Jeremiah said to Baruch, 'Look, I'm basically banned. I can't go into the Temple. So you have to go for me. Go on a fast day when there's a big crowd and read everything you wrote down from my dictation. Make sure all the people who travel in from the villages of Judah hear it too.'
'Maybe, just maybe, they'll start praying and God will actually listen. Maybe they'll turn away from their bad choices. This is no joke. God has made it crystal clear how seriously angry he is!'
Baruch, son of Neriah, did exactly what the prophet Jeremiah told him to. He went to the Temple of God and read God's Message from the scroll.
So, it was December in the fifth year of King Jehoiakim's rule. All the people from Jerusalem, plus everyone from the surrounding Judean towns, were in Jerusalem for a fast to honor God.

Baruch brought the scroll to the Temple and read Jeremiah's words out loud for everyone. He was in the office of Gemariah, the secretary of state, which was in the upper court right by the New Gate of the Temple. Literally everyone could hear him.

When Micaiah, who was Gemariah's son, heard what was being read from the scroll—God's actual message!—he went straight to the king's palace. He went to the secretary of state's office where all the government officials were having a meeting: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah, Elnathan, Gemariah, Zedekiah, and all the other officials.
Micaiah told them everything he had heard Baruch read from the scroll while they all listened.
Right away, they sent a guy named Jehudi to Baruch with an order: 'Take the scroll you read to the people and bring it here.' So Baruch went and got the scroll.
The officials said to him, 'Sit down. Read it to us, please.' And Baruch read it to them.
After they heard the whole thing, they were shook. They looked at each other and were like, 'We have to tell the king about this.'
They asked Baruch, 'Tell us, how did you write all this? Did Jeremiah dictate it to you?'
Baruch said, 'Yup. Every single word, straight from his mouth. And I wrote it down, word for word, with pen and ink.'
The officials told Baruch, 'You and Jeremiah need to disappear. Go hide. And don't let a single person know where you are!'

After stashing the scroll in the office of Elishama the secretary of state for safekeeping, the officials went to the king's court to report. The king sent Jehudi to get the scroll. He brought it from Elishama's office, and then Jehudi read it to the king and all the officials who were there with him.

It was December, so the king was chilling in his winter house in front of a fire. Every time Jehudi read three or four columns, the king would just take his little knife, cut that part off the scroll, and toss it into the fire. He kept doing this until the entire scroll was just ashes.

It was wild. Neither the king nor any of his officials felt even a little bit bad as they listened to the messages. Three guys—Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah—tried to talk the king out of burning the scroll, but he just ignored them. He went right ahead and ordered Prince Jerahameel and two other guys to arrest Jeremiah the prophet and his secretary Baruch. But God had them hidden.

After the king burned the scroll that Baruch had written from Jeremiah's dictation, God's message came to Jeremiah again: 'Get another blank scroll and do it all over. Write down everything that was on the first scroll that King Jehoiakim of Judah burned.'

'And give this personal message to King Jehoiakim of Judah: 'God says, You had the audacity to burn this scroll and then say, “What is this nonsense written here—that the king of Babylon will come and destroy this land and kill everyone?”'

'Well, you wanna know what God says about you, King Jehoiakim? This: None of your descendants will ever sit on David's throne. Your dead body will be thrown out on the street, left to rot in the hot sun and freeze in the cold night. I'm going to punish you, your kids, and your government officials for your obvious sin. I'm about to unleash the total disaster I warned you all about—the one you all just spat at.'

So Jeremiah went and got another scroll and gave it to his secretary, Baruch. At Jeremiah's dictation, he wrote down everything that King Jehoiakim had burned in the fire. And this time, they added a bunch of other stuff just like it.

title: Prophet Gets Jailed for Telling the Truth
paragraphs: So, King Zedekiah, Josiah's son, was on the throne. But get this: he was basically a puppet for Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon. He replaced King Jehoiachin son of Jehoiakim. The crazy part is, Zedekiah, his crew, and pretty much everyone else completely ignored the message God sent through the prophet Jeremiah.
But then, King Zedekiah sends two guys, Jehucal and Zephaniah, to Jeremiah with a message: 'Yo, you gotta pray for us. Like, for real, pray hard to our God.'

Back then, Jeremiah was still just chilling, walking around freely. This was all before he got thrown in jail. Meanwhile, Pharaoh's army was rolling in from Egypt. The Babylonians (aka the Chaldeans) who were attacking Jerusalem heard the Egyptians were on their way and were like, 'Aight, let's dip for a sec.'

Then God gave Jeremiah a message. He was like, 'Alright, go tell the king of Judah, the one who just sent for you, what's up. Tell him this: That Egyptian army coming to 'help' you? Yeah, they're not gonna stay. They'll show up and then bounce right back to Egypt. And then the Babylonians will come back, restart their attack, take over the city, and burn it all down. I'm God, and I'm telling you: don't play yourselves thinking the Babylonians are just gonna leave. They are not leaving. For real, even if you beat their whole army and only a few wounded soldiers were left in their tents, those wounded guys would still get up and burn this city to the ground.'

When the Babylonian army pulled back from Jerusalem, Jeremiah tried to leave the city to go to the Benjamin area to handle some family business. But when he got to the Benjamin Gate, the guard on duty, a guy named Irijah, grabbed him and accused him, 'You're trying to desert and join the Babylonians!'
'That's a lie!' Jeremiah shot back. 'I would never desert to the Babylonians.'

But Irijah wasn't hearing it. He arrested Jeremiah and took him to the officials. The officials were super mad at Jeremiah. They beat him up and threw him in a makeshift jail in the house of a guy named Jonathan the secretary. So Jeremiah ended up in this underground cell, basically a dungeon, and he was stuck there for a long time.
Later, King Zedekiah secretly sent for Jeremiah. The king asked him privately, 'So... any message from God?'
'Oh, there's a message alright,' Jeremiah said. 'You're gonna be handed over to the king of Babylon.'

Jeremiah didn't stop there. He went on, 'Can you even tell me why you threw me in prison? What did I do to you or your officials or anyone? And where are all your prophets now? The ones who kept saying the king of Babylon would never attack you or this land? Please, my king, listen to me! Don't send me back to that dungeon at Jonathan's house. I'll literally die there!'

So King Zedekiah ordered for Jeremiah to be moved to the palace courtyard. They gave him a loaf of bread from Bakers' Alley every day until the whole city ran out of bread. And that's where Jeremiah stayed, in the courtyard of the palace guards.

title: Stuck in the Mud (Literally)
paragraphs: So, these four officials—Shephatiah, Gedaliah, Jucal, and Pashur—heard what Jeremiah was telling everyone.

He was saying, 'This is God's message: Anyone who stays in this city will die. You'll either be killed in battle, starve, or get a deadly disease. But anyone who surrenders to the Babylonians will get to live. You'll escape with your life.'
'And God's word is final: This city is going to be handed over to the Babylonian army. They're gonna take it.'

These officials went straight to the king and said, 'You have to execute this man. He's seriously killing the morale of the soldiers and everyone else left in the city with his talk. This guy isn't trying to help us; he's trying to ruin us!'
King Zedekiah just gave in. 'Fine. Do whatever you want with him. I'm powerless against you guys.'

So they took Jeremiah and threw him into a cistern—a deep, dry well—that belonged to the king's son, Malkijah. It was in the courtyard of the palace guard. They used ropes to lower him down. There was no water, just a thick layer of mud at the bottom, and Jeremiah sank into it.

But then Ebed-melek, an Ethiopian official in the royal palace, heard that they had tossed Jeremiah into the cistern. The king was holding court at the Benjamin Gate, so Ebed-melek rushed from the palace and said to him, 'My lord the king, what these men have done is a huge crime! They've thrown Jeremiah the prophet into a cistern and are just leaving him there to starve to death. There's literally no bread left in the city.'
So the king ordered Ebed-melek, 'Take three men with you and go pull the prophet Jeremiah out of that cistern before he dies.'

Ebed-melek took three men and went to a storeroom in the palace. He grabbed some old rags and worn-out clothes, tied them together, and lowered them down to Jeremiah with ropes. Ebed-melek yelled down, 'Put these old rags under your armpits to pad the ropes.'
Jeremiah did it.
And just like that, they pulled him up with the ropes and got him out of the cistern. But he was still kept as a prisoner in the courtyard of the palace guard.

Later, King Zedekiah secretly sent for Jeremiah and had him brought to the third entrance of the Temple of God. The king said, 'I'm going to ask you something. Don't hide anything from me. Tell me the truth.'
Jeremiah replied, 'If I tell you the truth, you'll just have me killed. And besides, no matter what I say, you're not going to listen anyway.'
But Zedekiah made a secret promise to Jeremiah. 'As surely as the Lord who gave us life is living, I will not kill you or hand you over to the men who want you dead.'

So Jeremiah told Zedekiah, 'This is the message from the Lord God Almighty, the God of Israel: If you surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, you will live, this city won't be burned down, and you and your family will survive. But if you refuse to surrender, this city will be handed over to the Babylonians, and they will burn it to the ground. And you won't escape.'
King Zedekiah said, 'But I'm scared of the Judeans who have already deserted and joined the Babylonians. If I surrender, they'll hand me over to them, and they'll torture me.'

Jeremiah promised, 'They won't get you. Just listen to God's voice. I'm telling you what's best for you so that you can live. But if you refuse to surrender, God has shown me what will happen: Imagine all the women left in your palace being led out to the Babylonian officers, and they're all singing this song about you:
'"Your good friends totally played you and led you on. Now you're stuck knee-deep in mud, and your so-called friends are nowhere to be found."

'They will take all your wives and children and hand them over to the Babylonians. And you? You won't get away either. The king of Babylon will capture you, and then this whole city will be burned to the ground.'

Zedekiah told Jeremiah, 'Don't tell a soul about this conversation, or you're dead. If the officials hear that I talked with you and come ask what we said, just tell them you were begging me not to send you back to Jonathan's dungeon to die.'

And that's exactly what happened. The officials came to Jeremiah and questioned him, and he gave them the story the king had told him to. So they left him alone, since no one had actually overheard their conversation.
Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the palace guard until the day Jerusalem was finally captured.

title: Zedekiah's Epic Fail & Jeremiah's Surprise Rescue
paragraphs: So, in the ninth year Zedekiah was king, in the tenth month, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon rolled up with his whole army and surrounded Jerusalem, ready to take over. By the eleventh year, fourth month, and ninth day of Zedekiah's rule, they broke through the city's defenses.

All of Babylon's top officials came in and set up their command center right in the Middle Gate. You had guys like Nergal-sharezer of Simmagar, Nebushazban the Rabsaris, another Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag, and all the other big shots from Babylon.

When King Zedekiah and his last few soldiers saw this, they totally panicked and tried to escape. They snuck out at night through a path in the king's garden, went through a gate between two walls, and made a run for the wilderness, heading toward the Jordan Valley. But the Babylonian army was right on them and caught Zedekiah in the Jericho wilderness. They grabbed him and dragged him to King Nebuchadnezzar in Riblah in the land of Hamath. Nebuchadnezzar was not playing around. He made Zedekiah watch as he executed all of his sons, and then he killed all of Judah's nobles right in front of him. After making him watch all that horror, Nebuchadnezzar had Zedekiah's eyes gouged out, put him in chains, and shipped him off to Babylon.

Meanwhile, the Babylonians were going wild. They burned down the king's palace, the Temple, and everyone's houses. They tore down Jerusalem's walls. Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, rounded up everyone who was left in the city, plus anyone who had surrendered, and sent them all into exile in Babylon. The only people he didn't take were the super poor who had nothing. He just left them in Judah with some vineyards and fields to try and survive.

But here's a twist: King Nebuchadnezzar gave a special order to his captain, Nebuzaradan, about Jeremiah. He was like, "Find that guy Jeremiah and look after him. Make sure nothing bad happens to him, and give him whatever he wants."

So, Nebuzaradan and the other top Babylonian officers sent for Jeremiah. They got him out of the courtyard where he was being held and put him in the care of Gedaliah, son of Ahikam. Gedaliah was supposed to take him home safely. And just like that, Jeremiah got to go back and live among his people.

Just before all this went down, while Jeremiah was still locked up, God had given him a message. He was told: "Go talk to Ebed-melek the Ethiopian. Tell him that God, the God of Israel, says, 'Listen up. I'm about to do what I said I would to this city—and it's not gonna be good news. You'll be there to see it all happen. But on that day, I'm gonna rescue you. You won't be handed over to the guys you're so scared of. For real, I will save you. You won't die. You'll get out of this alive, all because you trusted me.' That's a promise from God."

title: Jeremiah's Free... But Now What? 😬
paragraphs: So, here's the deal with Jeremiah. God's message came to him *after* Nebuzaradan, the head honcho of the guard, let him go at Ramah. When this captain found him, Jeremiah was literally in chains with all the other people from Jerusalem and Judah being dragged off to Babylon.

The captain pulled Jeremiah aside and was like, "Look, your God said this place was gonna get wrecked. And He actually did it, because you all sinned against Him and wouldn't listen. So, yeah, this is what happens."

"But for you, Jeremiah," he said, "I'm taking off these chains. You're free. If you wanna roll with me to Babylon, cool, come on. I'll make sure you're good. But if you're not feeling Babylon, that's fine too. The whole country is wide open for you. Go wherever you want. If you wanna stay, go hang with Gedaliah, son of Ahikam. The king of Babylon put him in charge of the towns here. You can live with him and the people who are left. Or just, you know, do your own thing. Your call."
The captain even gave him some snacks for the road and a going-away present before sending him off.
Jeremiah decided to go to Gedaliah at Mizpah and just live with him and the people who got left behind in the country.

Meanwhile, all the army leaders and their soldiers who were hiding out in the fields heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah as the new governor. He was in charge of all the men, women, and children who were the poorest of the poor and hadn't been exiled to Babylon. So they all came to meet Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael, Johanan and Jonathan, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai, and Jaazaniah, along with their crews.
Gedaliah promised them, "You have nothing to fear from the Babylonian officials. Just stay here on the land and be subject to the king of Babylon. You'll be fine, for real."

"My job is to stay here in Mizpah and be your representative with the Babylonians when they show up. Your job is to take care of the land: make wine, harvest the summer fruits, press olive oil. Store it all up and settle into the towns you've taken over."

All the Judeans who had escaped to places like Moab, Ammon, and Edom heard that the king of Babylon had left a few survivors in Judah and made Gedaliah their governor. So they all started coming back to Judah from all the places they'd been scattered. They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and went to work, gathering a huge supply of wine and summer fruits.

One day, Johanan and all the army officers who had been hiding out came to Gedaliah at Mizpah and told him, "Hey, you know that Baalis, the king of Ammon, has sent Ishmael to kill you, right?" But Gedaliah didn't believe them.

Then Johanan took Gedaliah aside privately. "Let me go and kill Ishmael. No one needs to know about it. Why should we let him kill you and throw the whole country into chaos? Why let everyone you've gathered be scattered and what's left of Judah be destroyed?"
But Gedaliah told Johanan, "Don't do it. I forbid it. You're spreading a false rumor about Ishmael."

title: Massacre at Mizpah: A Wild Betrayal Story
paragraphs: So, in the seventh month, this guy Ishmael, son of Nethaniah and grandson of Elishama, showed up. He was a legit royal and had been one of the king's top guys. He rolled up to Mizpah with ten of his crew to visit Gedaliah, son of Ahikam. But while they were all eating together, Ishmael and his men suddenly jumped up, attacked Gedaliah, and killed him—yep, they killed the very guy the king of Babylon had put in charge. And it wasn't just Gedaliah— Ishmael also killed all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, plus the Chaldean soldiers stationed there.
And it didn't stop there. Ishmael also murdered all the Judeans who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, plus the Babylonian soldiers who were stationed there.

On the second day after Gedaliah's murder—and nobody knew about it yet—eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria. They had shaved their beards, torn their clothes, and cut themselves up, which was how people showed they were grieving. They were on a pilgrimage, bringing offerings to the Temple in Jerusalem.
Ishmael went out from Mizpah to meet them, putting on a big show of crying. When he met them, he was like, “Come on in, guys, come meet Governor Gedaliah.”

But as soon as they were inside the city, Ishmael and his goons slaughtered all the pilgrims and dumped their bodies into a big cistern. However, ten of the guys managed to save themselves. They cut a deal with Ishmael, saying, “Yo, don’t kill us! We’ve got a secret stash of wheat, barley, olive oil, and honey out in the fields.” So Ishmael backed off and didn’t kill them along with the others.

The whole reason Ishmael used the cistern was to hide the bodies and cover up that he'd killed Gedaliah. This cistern was actually built way back by King Asa to defend against King Baasha of Israel. That's the cistern Ishmael filled up with all the people he murdered.

Then Ishmael rounded up everyone else left in Mizpah as prisoners. This included the king's daughters who had been left in Gedaliah's care by Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard. After grabbing all the prisoners, Ishmael started heading toward the land of Ammon.
When Johanan, son of Kareah, and the other army officers with him heard about the messed-up stuff Ishmael had done, they immediately went after him. They caught up with him at the big pool in Gibeon.

When all the prisoners Ishmael had taken from Mizpah saw Johanan and his officers, they were lowkey shocked and so relieved. They all switched sides and joined Johanan to head back home. But Ishmael, the snake, managed to get away from Johanan with eight of his men and escaped to Ammon.
After that, Johanan and his officers gathered up all the people Ishmael had taken from Mizpah after killing Gedaliah—the men, women, kids, and officials—and brought them back from Gibeon.

They immediately started heading to Egypt to get away from the Babylonians, stopping on the way at a place called Geruth-kimham near Bethlehem. They were terrified of what the Babylonians would do when they found out that Ishmael had murdered Gedaliah, the governor they had appointed.

title: Stay or Go? God's Risky Advice
paragraphs: So all the army leaders, with Johanan and Jezaniah in charge, and pretty much everyone else, from the honored ones to the regular folks, went to the prophet Jeremiah. They said, “Yo, we need a favor. Please listen. Can you pray to your God for us, for what’s left of our crew? You can see there aren’t many of us. Ask your God to tell us where we should go and what we should do.”
Jeremiah the prophet replied, “I got you. I’ll pray to your God just like you asked. Whatever God says, I’ll pass it on to you. I’ll tell you everything, no holding back.”

They told Jeremiah, “We swear to God, and may He be a true and faithful witness against us if we don’t do every single thing that your God tells you to tell us. Whether we like it or not, we’ll do it. We’ll obey whatever our God tells us. Yeah, for real, you can count on us. We’ll do it.”
Ten days later, God’s message came to Jeremiah. He gathered Johanan son of Kareah and all the army officers with him, along with all the people, no matter how important they were.

Then he spoke: “This is the message from God, the God of Israel, the one you sent me to pray to. He says, ‘If you’re willing to stick it out in this land, I will build you up, not tear you down. I will plant you, not pull you up like a weed. I feel super bad about the disaster I brought on you. You don’t have to be afraid of the king of Babylon. Your fears are for nothing. I’m on your side, ready to save and deliver you from whatever he might do. I’ll show you mercy. And what’s more, he will show you mercy too! He’ll let you come back to your own land.’

“But don’t you dare say, ‘We’re not staying here,’ and refuse to obey your God’s command. Don’t say, ‘Nah, we’re going to Egypt, where it’s peaceful—no wars, no enemy attacks, and plenty of food. We’re gonna live there.’ If that’s the plan for what’s left of Judah, then listen to God’s message. This is what the Lord of Heaven’s Armies says: ‘If you’re determined to go to Egypt and make it your home, then the very wars you’re scared of will find you in Egypt, and the starvation you’re worried about will follow you to Egypt. And you’ll die there! Every last one of you who is set on going to Egypt to live there will be killed, starve, or get sick and die. No one will survive, not a single person! No one will escape the disaster I’m going to bring on you.’

“This is the message from the Lord of Heaven’s Armies, the God of Israel: ‘Just like I unleashed my anger and fury on the people of Jerusalem, I’ll do it all over again in Egypt. You’ll end up being a cursed, hated, and mocked joke. And you’ll never see your homeland again.’
“God has told you straight up, you survivors of Judah, ‘Don’t go to Egypt.’ Could it be any clearer? I’m warning you today that you’re living in a fantasy. You’re making a huge, fatal mistake.
“Didn’t you just send me to your God, saying, ‘Pray for us to our God. Tell us everything that God says and we’ll do it all’?

“Well, now I’ve told you, I’ve told you everything he said, and you haven’t obeyed a single word of it, not one thing your God sent me to tell you. So now, let me tell you what’s going to happen next: You’ll be killed, you’ll starve to death, you’ll get sick and die in that wonderful country where you’ve decided to go and live.”

title: They Straight Up Ignored God
paragraphs: So, Jeremiah just finished telling everyone the message God sent him to deliver—like, the whole thing. And then this dude Azariah, son of Hoshaiah, and Johanan, son of Kareah, with all their arrogant buddies, straight up said to Jeremiah, 'You're lying! God never sent you to tell us not to go to Egypt. This is all Baruch's idea, isn't it? He's trying to turn you against us and hand us over to the Babylonians to be killed or exiled.'
Johanan, the army officers, and pretty much everyone else just completely ignored God's message to stay in Judah.

So Johanan and the army officers rounded up everyone who was left in Judah, all the people who had come back from being scattered. We're talking men, women, kids, the king's daughters—everyone that Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had left with Gedaliah. And yeah, they also grabbed Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch. They totally disobeyed God and went to Egypt, ending up in the city of Tahpanhes.

While they were in Tahpanhes, God's word came to Jeremiah: 'Grab some big rocks and bury them in the mortar near the pavement leading to Pharaoh's building in Tahpanhes. Make sure some of the guys from Judah are watching.'

'Then tell them, 'This is what the LORD of Heaven's Armies says: Watch out! I'm sending for my servant, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. He's going to set up his throne right on top of these stones I had you bury, and he'll spread his canopy over them. He's coming to completely wreck Egypt. Some will die, some will be exiled, and some will be killed. He'll burn down the temples of Egypt's gods, and either burn the gods themselves or drag them off as loot. He'll pick Egypt clean like a shepherd picking lice off his clothes, and then just walk away without a scratch. He'll smash the sacred pillars at the temple of the sun in Egypt and set all the temples of their gods on fire.'

title: God's Final Warning: Don't Mess with Fake Gods
paragraphs: So, this is the message Jeremiah got for all the Judeans living in Egypt, in places like Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros. God, the Lord of armies, the God of Israel, said: 'You guys literally saw the disaster I brought down on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah. Look at them now—they're ghost towns, just rubble and smoking ruins. And it's all because they went down a dark path, making me angry by sacrificing and worshiping these new so-called gods that they, you, and your ancestors knew nothing about. I sent my servants, the prophets, to you guys over and over, day and night, begging you, 'Please, don't do this disgusting stuff that I absolutely hate.' But did anyone listen or turn back from their evil ways and stop sacrificing to these fake gods? Not a single one. So I unleashed my fury, a firestorm of anger on the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, leaving them in the ruined and wasted state they're still in today.'

'This is the message from God, the Lord of armies, the God of Israel: 'So why are you destroying your own lives? You're cutting yourselves off—men, women, children, and babies—from Judah, leaving yourselves totally isolated. And why are you making me so mad by sacrificing to these fake gods in Egypt, where you've chosen to live? You're only going to destroy yourselves and become a joke and a curse word to all the nations on earth.'

'Have you already forgotten the evil your ancestors did? And the evil of the kings of Judah and their wives? Not to mention your own evil, and your wives' evil, that you all showed off in Judah and Jerusalem? To this day, you haven't shown any regret or respect. Nobody cares about my teachings or the rules I laid out so clearly for you and your parents! So, this is what the Lord of armies has decided:

'Watch out! I've decided to bring disaster on you and wipe out everyone from Judah. I'm going to take what's left of Judah, those who insisted on going to Egypt to live, and I'll finish them off right there. In Egypt, they'll either be killed in battle or starve to death. It doesn't matter if you're a big shot or a nobody; you'll either be killed or starve. You'll end up as a cursed, hated, and mocked people. I'll punish those in Egypt just like I punished those in Jerusalem: with war, famine, and disease. None of the survivors who fled Judah for Egypt will ever make it back to Judah, the land they're so homesick for. No one will return, except maybe a handful of refugees.'

Then the men who knew their wives were burning incense to other gods, along with a big crowd of women and pretty much everyone else living in Pathros, Egypt, shot back at Jeremiah: 'We're not listening to this 'message from God' you're giving us. We're going to do what we want and keep sacrificing to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her. That's what our ancestors, our kings, and our leaders did back in the good old days in Judah and Jerusalem. We had plenty of food, life was good, and we had no problems. But as soon as we stopped sacrificing to the Queen of Heaven, everything went wrong. We've had nothing but war and starvation ever since.'

And the women added, 'Exactly! We're going to keep sacrificing to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out offerings to her. Our husbands are totally cool with it. They're fine with us making cakes shaped like her and pouring out offerings.'

Then Jeremiah confronted all the people, both men and women, who had answered him so rudely. He said, 'All those sacrifices you, your parents, your kings, your officials, and all the people of the land offered in the cities of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem—you think God didn't notice? Oh, he noticed. And he got sick of it. Finally, he couldn't stand your evil and disgusting actions anymore. That's why your land became a wasteland, a place of death, a horror story, a ghost town. And it still is. This disaster happened to you because you kept offering those sacrifices and sinned against God! You refused to listen to him or follow his instructions and the terms of his covenant.'

Jeremiah wasn't finished. He turned to the women and said, 'Listen up, all you people from Judah who are living in Egypt—listen to God's Word. The Lord of armies, the God of Israel, says: 'You women said it, and you did it. You said, 'We're going to keep our promises to sacrifice to the Queen of Heaven and pour out offerings to her, and no one can stop us!''

'Well, go on then. Keep your promises. Go all out. But listen to what God has to say about it, all you from Judah living in Egypt: 'I swear by my great name,' says God, 'that my name will never again be spoken in a vow by anyone from Judah in the whole land of Egypt, no one will say, 'As surely as the Lord God lives!' I'm watching every one of you, and I'm bringing disaster, not good.'

'All the Judeans in Egypt will die from war or starvation until they're all gone. The very few who escape from Egypt and make it back to Judah will be a tiny number. Then the small group that left Judah to live in Egypt will know whose words came true—mine or theirs.'

'And here's the proof: I will punish you right here, so you'll know that my warnings of disaster are real. Watch for this sign: I will hand over Pharaoh Hophra, the king of Egypt, to his enemies who want to kill him, just like I handed over King Zedekiah of Judah to his enemy, Nebuchadnezzar, who was hunting him down.'

title: When Life Hits Hard, God's Got You
paragraphs: So this is what Jeremiah told Baruch back in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim's rule, while Baruch was writing down everything Jeremiah was saying.

"This is a message from God, the God of Israel, straight to you, Baruch. You've been saying, 'I'm so done with this! It's just one bad thing after another. God's just piling on the struggles. I'm completely burned out and there's no end in sight.'

"But God's response is this: 'Yo, look around. Everything I've built, I'm about to tear down. Everything I've planted, I'm about to rip up. And I'm doing this everywhere, all over the world! So, don't be trying to make big moves for yourself right now. Things are gonna get way worse before they get any better. But for real, don't even worry. I'm gonna make sure you get through all of it alive.'"

title: Egypt's Epic Fail: God's Smackdown
paragraphs: Alright, so here's the word from God, delivered by the prophet Jeremiah, about the nations that don't roll with Him. This part's about Egypt. King Neco's army was chilling by the Euphrates River at Carchemish when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon rolled up and wrecked them. This was back when Jehoiakim was king of Judah, in his fourth year.

God was like, 'Yo, get ready for a fight! Grab your shields, get on your horses, helmets on, spears out, armor up!' But then, plot twist! I look over and they're all totally panicking. They're ditching their positions and scrambling. The soldiers are in full-on panic mode, running around like headless chickens. It's pure chaos, danger all over the place. That's what God said.
'The fastest runners? Not getting away. The strongest soldiers? Not escaping. Up north, by the Euphrates River, they're all just gonna trip and fall.'

So who's this, flooding in like the Nile River, all torrential and crazy? Oh, it's Egypt, acting like a massive flood, saying, 'I'm gonna take over the world, wipe out cities and everyone in them.' So the horses are running, the chariots are rolling, and the soldiers from Cush, Put, and Lud are marching out with their shields and bows.

But plot twist again, it's not their day. It's my day, says the Lord, God of the Angel Armies. This is the day I get even with my enemies. The day the Sword ends them, gets some serious payback. I, the Lord, God of the Angel Armies, am gonna offer them up like a huge sacrifice, way up north by the Euphrates.

'Yo, virgin Daughter Egypt, go get some healing lotion from Gilead. It won't matter though. You can try all the medicines you want, but nothing's gonna fix you. The whole world is gonna hear you crying. Your screams are gonna fill the earth as your soldiers trip over each other and go down in a huge pile.'
This is the message God gave to Jeremiah the prophet when King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon was about to throw down with Egypt:
'Shout it out in Egypt, give a heads-up in Migdol, post warnings in Noph and Tahpanhes: 'Wake up! Get ready! A war is coming!'

'Why is your bull-god Apis gonna bounce? Because God's gonna make him. Your whole messy army is gonna fall apart. The soldiers are all whispering, 'Let's dip while we can. Let's go home and save ourselves.' When they get back, they'll have a new nickname for Pharaoh: 'All-Talk-No-Action.' As sure as I'm the living God'—this is a decree from the King, whose name is God-of-the-Angel-Armies—'a conqueror is coming. He's gonna be unmissable, like Mount Tabor among the mountains, or Mount Carmel by the sea! So pack your stuff for exile, you pampered princesses of Egypt, because Memphis is about to become a ghost town, totally empty and overgrown.'

'Too bad, Egypt. You're like a pretty cow, and a horsefly from the north is about to mess you up. All your hired soldiers, who look like well-fed calves, are supposed to defend you. But when things get real, they're all gonna run away like total cowards. When it gets tough, they'll just take the easy way out.'

'Egypt's gonna hiss and slither away like a snake when the enemy army rolls in. They'll come at you with axes, like they're chopping down a forest. They're gonna flatten the whole country'—God's decree—'until there's nothing left as far as you can see. The invaders will be like a swarm of locusts, way too many to count. Daughter Egypt is gonna get wrecked, totally taken over by those vandals from the north.'

God-of-the-Angel-Armies, the God of Israel, says, 'Watch out, because I'm about to bring the pain to the god Amon of Thebes, to Egypt, its gods, its kings, to Pharaoh, and everyone who trusts him. I'm gonna hand them over to the people who want them dead, to King Nebuchadnezzar and his army. Egypt's gonna be set back like a thousand years. But eventually, people will live there again.' That's God's decree.

'But you, my boy Jacob, my servant, you don't have to be scared. Israel, no need to worry. Look! I'm gonna save you from that faraway country, and I'll get your kids out of exile. Things are gonna get back to normal for Jacob. You'll be safe and secure, smooth sailing from here. Yeah, my dear servant Jacob, don't be afraid. For real, I'm on your side. I'm gonna totally finish off all the nations where I scattered you, but I'm not gonna finish you. I've still got more work to do with you. I'll have to discipline you, but I'll be fair about it. Nah, I'm not done with you yet.'

title: God's Sword vs. The Philistines... It's a Sweep
paragraphs: This is the message God gave to Jeremiah the prophet about the Philistines, right before Pharaoh went and attacked Gaza. Here's what God said:

"Yo, look out! There's a flood of trouble coming from the north, and it's gonna be massive. It's going to completely swamp the land, taking out cities and everyone in them. People are gonna be screaming in total panic, you'll hear cries from every single house. The sound of horse hooves will be like thunder, chariots clattering, wheels banging—it's gonna be chaos. Dads will be so freaked out they won't even have time to grab their own kids. It's basically game over for the Philistines. No one's coming to help Tyre and Sidon either. God's gonna finish off the Philistines, whatever's left of them from the island of Crete. Gaza is gonna get totally wrecked, and Ashkelon will be left speechless. You guys are seriously on your last legs. How long are you gonna keep fighting a losing battle?
People will be crying out, 'Oh, Sword of God, for real, how long are you gonna keep this up? Put it away! Haven't you done enough? Can't you just stop?'
But how can it stop when I, God, am the one who gave the order? I've commanded it to take down Ashkelon and the whole coast."

title: Moab's Epic Fail
paragraphs: Here's the word on Moab from the God of the Angel Armies, the God of Israel:

“It’s over for Nebo! Totally wrecked. Kiriathaim is humiliated and captured, the super-strong fortress is now just a pile of rubble, and Moab’s fame is just dust and ashes. A bunch of haters are plotting in Heshbon, like, ‘Yo, let’s just wipe Moab off the face of the earth.’ The city of Madmen is about to get silenced, with non-stop chaos. Listen! Someone’s screaming from Horonaim: ‘This is a disaster—a total catastrophe!’ Moab is gonna be shattered. You’ll hear their crying all the way down in Zoar. People are weeping as they go up the hill to Luhith, and on the way down from Horonaim, you can hear cries of pure devastation. Yo, run for your lives! Get out of there! You gotta be smart and survive in the wild! You thought your strong walls and all your cash would save you, right? Wrong. It’s not gonna help you now. Your main god, Chemosh, is gonna get dragged away, along with his priests and officials. A destroyer is gonna hit every single city. Not one will be left. The valleys will be ruined, the plateaus destroyed, just like I said. You might as well cover Moab with salt, 'cause nothing's growing there again. Its towns will be ghost towns. No one will ever live there again. If you do God's work carelessly, you're cursed, and you're also cursed if you don't go all in with the sword.

“Moab has had it easy for, like, ever—just chilling, never having to work, no drama, no struggles. They never had to grow up or even break a sweat. But that’s all in the past now. I’m about to give them a super tough job that’ll be a major reality check. It’s gonna shatter all their illusions. Moab will be so embarrassed of their god Chemosh, just like Israel was embarrassed of their Bethel calf-gods they thought were so great. How long are you gonna keep saying, ‘We’re so tough, we can beat anyone’? The destruction of Moab has already started. Their best young soldiers are already dead.” This is a decree from the King, whose full name is God-of-the-Angel-Armies. “Yep. Moab’s doom is on a countdown, the disaster has been targeted and launched. Cry for Moab, all you friends and neighbors who knew how famous it was. Say, ‘Wow, its mighty power is snapped in half like a toothpick, that amazing royal staff!’

“Get off your high horse, you pampered princess of Dibon. Go sit in some dirt. The one who destroys Moab is coming for you. He’s gonna wreck your safe and secure homes. Stand by the road, you privileged women of Aroer. Ask the refugees running away, ‘What happened? Why?’ Moab will be a cringey memory, with nothing left. Cry your eyes out! Tell everyone by the Arnon river the bad news. Tell the world that Moab is gone.

“My judgment is coming for all the plateau cities: Holon, Jahzah, Mephaath, Dibon, Nebo, Beth-diblathaim, Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon, Kerioth, Bozrah, and all the other cities in Moab, whether they're close by or far away.
“Moab’s power is cut off. Its strength is broken.” That's God's decree.

“Let’s get Moab wasted, drunk on my anger, so drunk they're covered in their own vomit—a total joke. Hey Moab, wasn't it you who made fun of Israel? When they got into trouble, didn't you just gossip and laugh at them?
“Leave your towns! Get out! Go live in the cliffs, you people from Moab. Be like a dove that builds its nest high up in a canyon.

“We’ve all heard about Moab’s pride, it's legendary. That arrogant, bullying, puffed-up pride, it's just too much. I know,” says God, “all that bragging, those empty claims, it’s all just a bunch of nothing. But I’m gonna cry for Moab, I’ll mourn for its people. I’ll even mourn for the people of Kir-heres. I’ll cry for the grapevines of Sibmah and weep with Jazer—grapevines that used to stretch all the way to the Dead Sea. Your summer fruit and grapes will be stolen by brutal enemies. Moab, once so full of life, will lose its joy and laughter. And yeah, I’m shutting down the winepresses, no more happy harvest shouts.
“Heshbon and Elealeh will scream, and people in Jahaz will hear it. They’ll hear it all the way from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. Even the waters of Nimrim will dry up.
“I’m putting a stop to Moab’s religious rituals,” says God, “no more hiking up to high places to burn sacrifices to their gods.
“My heart aches for Moab, for the men of Kir-heres, like a sad flute song. They’ve lost everything. They have nothing left.
“Everywhere you look, people are mourning: they’ve shaved their heads, cut their beards, scratched their hands, and torn their clothes.
“There will be loud crying in every house and on every street in Moab. I’m going to smash Moab to pieces like a clay pot that nobody wants.” That's God's decree.
“Moab is ruined! So embarrassed and ashamed! Moab is a cruel joke! The horror of Moab is so real!”
God’s final word on Moab. For real.

“Look! An eagle is about to dive down and spread its wings over Moab. The towns will be captured, the fortresses taken. Even the bravest warriors will be crying in pain, totally helpless, like a woman giving birth. There will be nothing left of Moab, absolutely nothing, because they were so arrogant and defiant against me.

“Terror, pits, and traps are what you’re facing, Moab.” That's God's decree. “If you run from the terror, you’ll fall into a pit. If you climb out of the pit, you’ll get caught in a trap. This is what I have planned for Moab on its judgment day.” That's God's decree.

“Refugees will stop on the edge of Heshbon, totally exhausted. A fire will shoot out from Heshbon, a huge firestorm from the capital of Sihon’s kingdom. It will burn off Moab’s eyebrows and scorch the skulls of those braggarts. It’s over for you, Moab! You worshipers of Chemosh are finished! Your sons will be taken to prison camps, and your daughters will be herded into exile. But one day, I will make things right in Moab again.
“But for now, that’s the judgment on Moab.”

title: God's Judgment on the Nations is Lowkey Wild
paragraphs: God’s message about the Ammonites:

“Yo, does Israel not have any kids or something? No one to inherit their stuff? So why is their god Milcom taking over Gad’s land, and his followers moving into its towns? But not for long! The time’s coming”—God’s decree—“when I’ll make Rabbah, Ammon’s big city, hear battle cries. It’ll end up as a pile of rubble, and all its towns will be burned to the ground. Then Israel will kick out the invaders. I, God, said it, so it’s gonna happen. Cry it out, Heshbon, ‘cause Ai is wrecked. You villages of Rabbah, freak out! Dress in black, cry your eyes out. Go nuts, run around like crazy! Your god Milcom is gonna get dragged into exile, with all his priests and managers right there with him. Why are you bragging about your strength that used to be famous? You’re a washed-up has-been, a total reject who’s just clinging to old trophies and dreaming about the good old days, thinking, ‘Nobody can touch me.’ Well, think again. I'm gonna bring the terror from all sides.” Word of the Master, God-of-the-Angel-Armies. “You’ll be stampeded and scattered, with no one to gather the runaways. Still, the time will come when I’ll make things right with Ammon.” God’s decree.
The message of God-of-the-Angel-Armies about Edom:

“Is there like, no one smart left in famous Teman? No one with a clue? Has their wisdom gone bad? Run for your lives! Get out while you can! Find a good hiding spot, you who live in Dedan! I’m bringing disaster to Esau. It’s payback time. When people harvest your fields, don’t they leave some leftovers? When burglars break in, don’t they just take what they want? But I’m gonna leave Esau with nothing. I’ll search every corner. I’ll destroy everything connected to him—his kids, relatives, and neighbors. There’ll be no one left to say, ‘I’ll take care of your orphans. Your widows can count on me.’”

For real. God says, “I’m telling you, if some people have to drink the cup of God’s anger even when they don’t deserve it, why would you think you’d get a pass? You won’t get a pass. You’ll drink it. Oh yeah, you’ll drink every last drop. And as for Bozrah, your capital, I swear by my own self”—God’s decree—“that city will become a pile of burnt ruins, a stinking garbage dump, a total disgrace—and all its surrounding towns with it.”
I just heard the latest from God. He sent a messenger to the nations: “Get your squad together and attack Edom. Gear up! Go to war!”

“Oh, Edom, I’m making you the weakest of all nations, the bottom of the barrel, totally disrespected. You think you’re so tough—strutting around all high and mighty, living in your fortress in the rocks, acting like you're king of the hill. You think you’re untouchable, right? Like an eagle in its nest? Well, you’re about to get knocked down. I’ll bring you crashing to the ground.” God’s decree.
“Edom will end up as straight-up garbage. Disgusting, nasty trash. A total train wreck. It’ll be just like Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors in the history books of failure.” God says so.
“No one will live there, not a single person will move in.

“Watch this: Like a lion creeping up from the Jordan jungle looking for a snack in the mountain pastures, I’ll jump Edom and pounce. I’ll take my pick of the flock—and who’s gonna stop me? The shepherds of Edom are helpless against me.”
So, listen to the plan God has made against Edom, the blueprint he’s prepared for those who live in Teman:

“Believe it or not, even the young and weak—like little lambs and kids—will be dragged off. Believe it or not, the flock will be in shock, totally helpless, and just watch it happen. The whole earth will shake from their cries, cries of pain heard all the way at the Red Sea. Look! An eagle soars, swoops down, and spreads its wings over Bozrah. Even the toughest warriors will be doubled over in pain, totally helpless, like a woman giving birth.”
The message about Damascus:

“Hamath and Arpad will be shook when they hear the bad news. Their hearts will melt with fear as they pace around, worried sick. The color will drain from Damascus’s face as she tries to run. Panicking, she’ll fall apart, totally disabled, like a woman in labor. And now, how lonely—left behind, abandoned! The once-famous city, the once-happy city. Her bright young men are dead in the streets, her brave warriors silent as death. On that day”—decree of God-of-the-Angel-Armies—“I’m gonna light up the walls of Damascus and burn down all of Ben-hadad’s forts.”
The message about Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor that were attacked by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. This is God’s message:

“Get up! Attack Kedar! Go plunder the nomads from the east. Grab their blankets and pots and pans. Steal their camels. Freak them out, shouting, ‘Terror! Death! Doom! Danger everywhere!’ Oh, run for your lives, you nomads from Hazor.” God’s decree. “Find a safe place to hide. Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has plans to wipe you out, to come after you with a vengeance: ‘Get ‘em,’ he says. ‘Go after these chill nomads who live free and easy in the desert, who live out in the open with no doors to lock, who live by themselves.’ Their camels are free for the taking, their herds and flocks, easy grabs. I’ll scatter them to the four winds, these defenseless nomads on the edge of the desert. I’ll bring terror from every direction. They won’t know what hit them.” God’s decree. “Jackals will take over the camps of Hazor, camps abandoned to the wind and sand. No one will live there, not a single person will move in.”
God’s message to the prophet Jeremiah about Elam at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah. This is what God-of-the-Angel-Armies says:

“Watch this! I’ll snap Elam’s bow, their favorite weapon, right over my knee. Then I’ll unleash four winds on Elam, winds from the four corners of the earth. I’ll blow them away in all directions, and homeless Elamites will end up in every country on earth. They’ll live in constant fear and terror among enemies who want to kill them. I’ll bring disaster on them, my anger-fueled disaster. I’ll send killer dogs after them until there’s nothing left. And then I’ll set up my throne in Elam, after kicking out their king and his cronies. But the time will come when I’ll make everything right for Elam again.” God’s decree.

title: Babylon's Epic Fail
paragraphs: This is the word God gave through the prophet Jeremiah about Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans:

“Alright, listen up, world! Tell everyone, shout it from the rooftops: Babylon is DONE. Their god Bel is so embarrassed, and Marduk is exposed as a total fake. All their little statues are cringing, and their fake gods are looking like cheap knock-offs. Because a nation from the north is gonna roll up and wreck their cities. It's gonna be a ghost town—no people, no animals, not a single sound.

“When that day comes,” God says, “the people of Israel and Judah are gonna come back together. They’ll be crying, but they’ll be looking for me, their God. They’ll ask for the way to Zion and head straight there. They’re gonna stick with God, making a forever-promise they’ll never forget.

“My people were like lost sheep. Their own shepherds messed them up and left them to wander in the mountains. They got so lost they forgot where home was. Anyone who found them just took advantage. Their enemies were like, ‘Whatever, it’s fine. They’re the ones who ditched God, the true home their ancestors trusted.’

“But now, you gotta bounce from Babylon, like, ASAP. Get out of that country. Don't just follow, be a leader. Lead the way home! You see what I'm doing? I'm gathering a whole squad of nations against Babylon. They're coming from the north to take it all. These armies don't play; they never leave empty-handed. Babylon is basically free real estate. All the looters are gonna eat good!” God declares.

“You Babylonians really lived it up, huh? You had a blast taking advantage of my people, like happy little calves in a field or wild horses having fun. Well, your mom wouldn't be proud. The one who gave birth to you would be disappointed. Look at you now! You're a nobody nation, just trash and weeds. My anger is gonna leave you totally empty, a lifeless desert. Anyone who passes by will be shook, like, ‘Wow, what a glow-down.’ So, gang up on Babylon! Surround her! Unleash everything you've got. Don't hold back. Take her down. She messed up big time, against me! Let out a battle cry from all sides. She's got no fight left. Her defenses are toast, her walls are smashed. This is ‘Operation: God’s Payback.’ Get that revenge. Do to her what she did to others. Give her a taste of her own medicine! Wreck her farms, get rid of her farmers, and empty her barns. And for all you prisoners, while it's all going down, get out of there. Run for your lives and go home.
“Israel is like a scattered flock of sheep, hunted by lions. The king of Assyria started it, and then King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon finished the job, leaving nothing but bones.”

And now, the God of Angel Armies, the God of Israel, says this: “Watch out. I’m about to bring the same level of doom on the king of Babylon and his country that I brought on the king of Assyria. But I’ll bring Israel back home to good pastures. They’ll chill on the hills of Carmel and Bashan, and on the slopes of Ephraim and Gilead. They’ll eat until they’re totally full. When that time comes,” God says, “people will search for any dirt on Israel, but they won’t find a thing. They’ll look for any of Judah’s sins, but nothing. The people I saved will have a totally clean slate.
“Attack Merathaim, the land of rebels! Go after Pekod, the country of doom! Hunt them down and wipe them out,” God decrees. “These are my orders. Do exactly what I say.

“The sound of battle is shaking everything! The big bad ‘Hammer’ just got hammered, totally smashed. Babylon is wrecked beyond recognition. I set a trap for you, Babylon, and you walked right into it. You had no idea what was coming. Now you’re caught. That’s what you get for trying to fight God.

“I, God, opened up my armory. I brought out my weapons of anger. The Master, the God of Angel Armies, has a job to do in Babylon. Attack it from every angle! Break into their storage! Pile everything up and burn it. Leave nothing and no one! Get rid of all their young fighters. It’s their doomsday! Their time is up. And get this: the people who escape from Babylon will show up in Zion and tell everyone how God got his revenge, especially for his Temple.

“Send all the troops against Babylon, anyone who’s a good shot! Trap them completely, no escape routes! Pay her back for everything she did. Give her a taste of her own medicine! She was so arrogant and disrespectful to God, the Holy One of Israel. So now it’s payback time: her young men will be found dead in the streets, and all her soldiers will be silenced forever,” God decrees.

“You getting this, Mr. Pride? I’m coming for you!” says the Master, the God of Angel Armies. “Your time is up. It’s your doomsday. Mr. Pride is gonna fall flat on his face, and no one’s gonna help him up. I’m gonna set his towns on fire, and it’s gonna spread everywhere.”
And here’s more from the God of Angel Armies:

“The people of Israel and Judah are both oppressed. Their enemies have them in a death grip and won’t let go. But their Rescuer is strong: the God of Angel Armies. I’m gonna step in and save them. I’ll bring peace to their land, but for the people of Babylon, it’s gonna get rough.

“It’s an all-out war in Babylon,” God says. “A total war on its people, its leaders, and its so-called wise men! War on its fake prophets—they’re all fools! War on its soldiers—they’re all cowards! War on its hired fighters—they’re useless! War on its banks—they’re getting looted! War on its water—it’s drying up! This land of fake gods has gone nuts—just a bunch of creepy goblins! The whole place will be taken over by wild animals and creepy crawlies. No one will ever live there again. It’ll smell like death. It’s gonna be like Sodom and Gomorrah, those cities I completely destroyed,” God says. “No one will ever live there again. No one will even breathe the air in that land, ever.

“And now, check this out! A huge crowd is coming from the north, a massive army of kings from all over the world. They’ve got deadly weapons, and they’re savage and cruel. They roar like the ocean, riding on powerful horses, all lined up and ready to fight you, Babylon! The king of Babylon hears they’re coming and gets so scared he can’t even move. He’s terrified, doubled over in pain like a woman giving birth.

“And watch this: like a lion coming out of the jungle to hunt in the mountains, I’m gonna show up and attack. I’ll take whoever I want from the flock, and who’s gonna stop me? All those so-called shepherds are completely powerless against me.”
So, listen up. This is God’s master plan against Babylon, the blueprint for what he’s gonna do to Chaldea:

Believe it or not, even the weakest, most vulnerable ones—like little lambs—will be dragged away. And the rest of the flock will just watch in shock, totally helpless. When everyone shouts, “Babylon is down!” the whole world will feel it. The news will spread everywhere.
