title: Babylon's Epic Takedown
paragraphs: Alright, there's more. God's dropping another truth bomb:

"Yo, watch this. I'm about to unleash a crazy destructive hurricane on Babylon—let's call it 'Hurricane Persia'—against everyone living in that messed-up place. I'm sending in a cosmic cleanup crew, and they're gonna scrub Babylon clean. Seriously, when they're done, there'll be nothing left worth mentioning. They won't miss a single thing. It's the final, total Doomsday. Soldiers will go all out, no holding back. They're not sparing anyone or anything. It's the end of the line, a complete wipeout. Babylon's streets will be littered with wounded people, just piles of bodies. But guess what? It turns out Israel and Judah aren't left all alone. As their God, the God of Angel Armies, I'm still here, totally committed to them, even though their country was filled with sin against Israel's Holy God.

"Get out of Babylon, like, right now. Run for your lives, save yourselves! Don't stick around and get caught up in my revenge on her. I'm just paying her back for all her bad choices. Babylon was like this fancy gold cup I was holding, filled with my anger that made the whole world drunk. All the nations drank from it and went totally wild. Now Babylon herself is gonna stumble and fall, completely wasted. So tragic! Go find some healing ointment for her wounds. Who knows, maybe she can be fixed."

"We tried our best, but she's a lost cause. Babylon is past the point of no return. Just leave her to her fate and go home. The judgment against her is gonna be massive, like a skyscraper-sized monument to my vengeance.
"God made everything right for us. Let's go! We've gotta tell everyone back in Zion the good news. Let's spread the word on what our God did to fix things.

"Sharpen your arrows! Get your quivers full! God has hyped up the kings of the Medes, giving them a serious case of war fever. The mission: 'Destroy Babylon!' God is on the warpath, out to get revenge for his Temple. Give the signal to attack Babylon's walls. Post guards 24/7. Call for backup. Set up ambushes. God's gonna do exactly what he said he would to the people of Babylon. You guys have all the water and money you could ever want—but your time is up. Your lifeline's been cut."
God of the Angel Armies has sworn a solemn oath: "I'm gonna fill this place with so many soldiers, they'll swarm like locusts, chanting victory songs right in your face."

With his power, he made the earth. His wisdom shaped the world. He's the master artist of the cosmos. When he thunders, rain pours down. He makes clouds soar, adds lightning to the storm for special effects, and unleashes the wind from his private stash. People who worship fake gods made of sticks look so foolish. The makers of these gods are just embarrassed by their own creations. Their gods are fakes, just dead pieces of wood—pathetic, tasteless jokes. They're nothing but smoke. When it clears, they're gone. But the God of Jacob is the real deal; he created the entire universe, and he gave special attention to Israel. His name? God-of-the-Angel-Armies!

God says, "You, Babylon, you're my hammer, my weapon of war. I'm gonna use you to smash godless nations and tear down kingdoms. I'll use you to wreck horse and rider, chariot and driver. I'll use you to take down man and woman, old man and boy. I'll use you to crush the young man and woman, the shepherd and his sheep. I'll use you to destroy the farmer and his oxen, and to take out governors and senators.
"Judeans, you're gonna see it all with your own eyes. I'll make Babylon and all the Chaldeans pay for the evil they did in Zion." That's a decree from God.

"I'm against you, Babylon, you 'Mount Destroyer,' you who wrecked the whole earth. I'm gonna reach out, grab you, and crush you until you're not a mountain anymore. I'll turn you into a gravel pit. No one will ever use your stones for important buildings again—no cornerstones, no foundation stones. You'll be nothing but gravel." That's God's decree.

"Raise a flag in the land, blow the trumpet for the nations. Get the nations ready for a holy war against her. Call the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz to fight. Appoint a commander, and bring in horses like a swarm of locusts! Get the nations ready for a holy war against her—the king of the Medes, his leaders, and all his people.

"The whole land is shaking in fear, terrified of my plans against Babylon. My plan is to turn Babylon into a lifeless wasteland, a total ghost town. Babylon's soldiers have just given up. They're hiding in caves like cowards who didn't even put up a fight. What a bunch of crybabies. Babylon's houses are on fire, its gates are busted. Messenger after messenger is running to the king of Babylon to tell him his city is totally done for. The river crossings are captured. Wildfires are burning through the swamps. Soldiers are deserting like crazy. I, the God-of-the-Angel-Armies, told you this would happen: 'Daughter Babylon is like a threshing floor at harvest time. Soon, her own harvest will come, and the useless stuff will be blown away!'

"King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon chewed up my people and spit out their bones. He cleaned his plate, pushed back his chair, and let out a huge, greedy burp. Lady Zion says, 'Let the same violence done to me be done to Babylon!' And Jerusalem says, 'Make the Chaldeans pay for the blood they spilled!' Then I, God, step in and say, 'I've got your back. I'm your Avenger. You'll get your revenge. I'll dry up her rivers and plug her springs. Babylon will become a pile of ruins, a hangout for stray dogs, a garbage dump, a ghost town that no one goes near.'

"The Babylonians will be like hungry lions, roaring for food. But I'll be the one making them a meal—a whole banquet, actually. They'll get so drunk they'll pass out. Dead drunk, they'll sleep... and sleep... and never wake up." That's God's decree. "I'll drag these 'lions' to the slaughterhouse like lambs and goats, and they'll never be heard from again.

"Babylon is done. The pride of the whole world has fallen flat on its face. What a major L for Babylon, ending up in the gutter. Babylon is drowned in chaos, getting slammed by waves of enemy soldiers. Her towns are rotting and decaying, the land is empty and barren. Nobody lives there anymore. People go way out of their way to avoid them. I'm gonna take down that glutton god, Bel, in Babylon. I'll make him puke up everything he swallowed. No more tourists will come to admire the 'wonders' of Babylon. The wonders are gone. Run for it, my people! Run and don't look back! Get out of this place while you still can, this place that's about to be torched by God's insane anger. Don't lose hope. Don't give up when you hear all the crazy rumors. One year it's this, the next it's that—rumors of violence and war. But trust me, the time is coming when I'll deal with Babylon's fake gods. I'll expose the whole country as a fraud, with dead bodies scattered everywhere. Heaven and earth, angels and people, will throw a massive victory party over Babylon when the avenging armies from the north come down on her." That's God's decree!

"Babylon has to fall—it's payback for all the people of Israel who died in the war. Babylonians will be killed because of all the killing they did. But you exiles who escaped being killed by Babylon, get out of there! Fast! Remember God, even though you're far from home. And don't forget Jerusalem."

"We've been so humiliated, mocked, and abused. We've been kicked around for so long we barely know who we are anymore. And we don't know what to think—our holy Temple, God's house, was desecrated by a bunch of strangers."

"I know, but trust me: The time is coming"—God's decree—"when I'll bring judgment on her fake idols, and all over this land, the wounded will be groaning in pain. Even if Babylon built a ladder to the moon and then pulled it up so no one could reach her, it wouldn't stop me. I'd make sure my avengers would get to her." That's God's decree.

"But listen! You hear that? It's a cry coming from Babylon! A wild scream from Chaldea! God is taking a wrecking ball to Babylon. We're about to hear her last noises—death cries that sound like crashing waves, death rattles like a roaring waterfall. The destroyer is about to enter Babylon. Her soldiers are captured, their weapons are broken. You see, God is a God who makes things even. Everyone gets what they deserve.

"I'm gonna get them all drunk—the princes, the wise men, the governors, the soldiers. They'll get so drunk they'll pass out... and sleep and sleep... and never wake up." That's a decree from the King. His name? God-of-the-Angel-Armies!
God-of-the-Angel-Armies says:

"Those massive walls of Babylon? They're gonna be completely flattened. And those huge city gates? They're gonna be set on fire. The harder you chase after this empty life, the less you have. All that ambition just turns to ashes."

Jeremiah the prophet gave a task to Seraiah, who was the son of Neriah and grandson of Mahseiah. This happened when Seraiah went with King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign. Seraiah was basically the trip coordinator.

Jeremiah had written down in a little book all the terrible things that were going to happen to Babylon. He told Seraiah, "When you get to Babylon, read this whole thing out loud in public. Read, 'You, O God, said you would destroy this place so that nothing could live here, not even people or animals—a total wasteland, an eternal nothing.'

"When you're done reading it, tie a rock to the book, throw it into the Euphrates River, and watch it sink. Then say, 'This is how Babylon will sink and never come back up after the disaster I'm bringing on her.'"

title: The Final Days of Jerusalem: It Gets Real
paragraphs: So, this guy Zedekiah was 21 when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for 11 years. His mom was Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah from a town called Libnah.
As far as God was concerned, Zedekiah was just another bad king, a total carbon copy of Jehoiakim.
Basically, all the terrible stuff that went down in Jerusalem and Judah was because God was just so angry. He pretty much turned his back on them as a final judgment.

Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. So, Nebuchadnezzar rolled up with his whole army. They set up camp and built siege ramps all around Jerusalem, completely sealing it off. This all started in the ninth year and tenth month of Zedekiah's rule. The city was under siege for a wild 19 months, all the way until Zedekiah's eleventh year as king.

By the fourth month of Zedekiah’s eleventh year, on the ninth day, the famine was insane. There wasn't a single crumb of bread for anyone. That's when the Babylonians finally broke through the city walls. In the middle of the night, the whole Judean army tried to escape through a gate between two walls near the King's Garden. They slipped past the Babylonian lines surrounding the city and made a run for the Jordan Valley. But the Babylonians were right on them. They caught up to Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, but by then his whole army had bailed on him and scattered.

The Babylonians captured Zedekiah and dragged him to the king of Babylon at Riblah in Hamath, who put him on trial and sentenced him right there. The king of Babylon made Zedekiah watch as he killed his sons. That was the last thing Zedekiah ever saw, because they blinded him right after. Then the king of Babylon killed all of Judah's officials too. Zedekiah was put in chains and hauled off to Babylon, where he was thrown in prison and stayed there until he died.

In the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, on the seventh day of the fifth month, his top commander, Nebuzaradan, showed up in Jerusalem. He burned God's Temple to the ground, then the royal palace, and then the rest of the city. He torched the whole place. He had his Babylonian troops tear down the city walls. Finally, he rounded up everyone left in the city, including the people who had already surrendered, and shipped them off to exile. He only left a few of the poorest farmers to take care of the vineyards and fields.

The Babylonians smashed the bronze pillars, the bronze washing stands, and the giant bronze basin called 'the Sea' that were in God's Temple, and they carried all the bronze away to Babylon. They also took all the bronze tools, and the gold and silver bowls and censers used in the Temple services. The commander didn't miss a thing; he took every piece of precious metal he could find.

The amount of bronze they got was insane. The two pillars, the Sea, the twelve bronze bulls that held it up, and the ten washstands that Solomon had made for the Temple of God—it was too much to even weigh. Each pillar was 27 feet tall and 18 feet around. They were hollow, with the bronze being just under an inch thick. On top of each pillar was a fancy bronze capital with pomegranates and detailed metalwork, adding another seven and a half feet to the height. There were 96 pomegranates spaced out, with a total of 100 woven into the design.

The commander also took some high-profile prisoners: Seraiah the head priest, Zephaniah the priest under him, three important guards, the top army officer who was left, seven of the king's advisors found in the city, the army's main recruiter, and sixty other important guys who were still around. Nebuzaradan marched them all to the king of Babylon at Riblah in Hamath. And right there in Riblah, the king of Babylon had them all executed in cold blood.
So Judah was forced into exile, kicked out of their own land.
In the seventh year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar took 3,023 people from Judah into exile.
In his eighteenth year, he took another 832 from Jerusalem.
Then in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year, his chief deputy Nebuzaradan took 745 more people from Judah.
The grand total of exiles was 4,600.

Thirty-seven years after King Jehoiachin of Judah was taken into exile, a new king, Evil-Merodach, came to power in Babylon. He let Jehoiachin out of prison on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month. The king was super nice to him, giving him way better treatment than any of the other royal prisoners in Babylon. Jehoiachin got to change out of his prison clothes and ate at the king's table for the rest of his life. The king gave him everything he needed to live comfortably until he died.
